raw: CHAPTER XXIV. Drawn to the Loadstone Rock
en: [Chapter 24] Drawn to the Loadstone Rock

raw: In such risings of fire and risings of sea--the firm earth shaken by the rushes of an angry ocean which had now no ebb, but was always on the flow, higher and higher, to the terror and wonder of the beholders on the shore--three years of tempest were consumed.
en: Three years of storm passed with these rising fires and rising seas, the steady earth shaken by the rushes of an angry ocean that never ebbed but kept rising higher and higher, terrifying and amazing everyone on the shore.

raw: Three more birthdays of little Lucie had been woven by the golden thread into the peaceful tissue of the life of her home.
en: During this time, three more birthdays of little Lucie were woven by the golden thread into the peaceful life of her home.

raw: Many a night and many a day had its inmates listened to the echoes in the corner, with hearts that failed them when they heard the thronging feet.
en: Many a night and day, the family listened to the echoes in the corner of their house, their hearts sinking when they heard the sound of marching feet.

raw: For, the footsteps had become to their minds as the footsteps of a people, tumultuous under a red flag and with their country declared in danger, changed into wild beasts, by terrible enchantment long persisted in.
en: In their minds, those footsteps had become the steps of a rioting mob under a red flag, their country declared in danger, transformed into wild beasts by a terrible spell of long-standing anger.

raw: Monseigneur, as a class, had dissociated himself from the phenomenon of his not being appreciated: of his being so little wanted in France, as to incur considerable danger of receiving his dismissal from it, and this life together.
en: The French aristocrats, as a class, had run away from the fact that they were no longer wanted in France, where they faced the danger of being kicked out of the country and of life itself.

raw: Like the fabled rustic who raised the Devil with infinite pains, and was so terrified at the sight of him that he could ask the Enemy no question, but immediately fled; so, Monseigneur, after boldly reading the Lord’s Prayer backwards for a great number of years, and performing many other potent spells for compelling the Evil One, no sooner beheld him in his terrors than he took to his noble heels.
en: Like the legendary peasant who worked hard to summon the Devil but was so terrified when he appeared that he fled without asking a single question, the aristocrats, after spending years doing everything to bring about disaster, ran away in fear the moment they saw the monster they had created.

raw: The shining Bull’s Eye of the Court was gone, or it would have been the mark for a hurricane of national bullets.
en: The glittering court of the King was gone, or else it would have been targeted by a storm of bullets.

raw: It had never been a good eye to see with--had long had the mote in it of Lucifer’s pride, Sardanapalus’s luxury, and a mole’s blindness--but it had dropped out and was gone.
en: It had never been a wise or observant court anyway, it had long been blinded by pride, luxury, and ignorance, but now it was completely gone.

raw: The Court, from that exclusive inner circle to its outermost rotten ring of intrigue, corruption, and dissimulation, was all gone together.
en: The royal court, from its inner circle to its outer rings of lies, corruption, and plotting, had vanished.

raw: Royalty was gone; had been besieged in its Palace and “suspended,” when the last tidings came over.
en: The monarchy was gone, having been besieged in the palace and suspended, according to the latest news.

raw: The August of the year one thousand seven hundred and ninety-two was come, and Monseigneur was by this time scattered far and wide.
en: By August of 1792, the French aristocrats were scattered far and wide.

raw: As was natural, the head-quarters and great gathering-place of Monseigneur, in London, was Tellson’s Bank.
en: Naturally, the main gathering place for these exiled French lords in London was Tellson's Bank.

raw: Spirits are supposed to haunt the places where their bodies most resorted, and Monseigneur without a guinea haunted the spot where his guineas used to be.
en: Just as ghosts are said to haunt the places they frequented in life, these penniless aristocrats hung around the place where their money used to be kept.

raw: Moreover, it was the spot to which such French intelligence as was most to be relied upon, came quickest.
en: It was also the spot where the most reliable news from France arrived quickest.

raw: Again: Tellson’s was a munificent house, and extended great liberality to old customers who had fallen from their high estate.
en: Tellson's was very generous to its old customers who had lost their wealth.

raw: Again: those nobles who had seen the coming storm in time, and anticipating plunder or confiscation, had made provident remittances to Tellson’s, were always to be heard of there by their needy brethren.
en: Furthermore, the nobles who had foreseen the storm and sent their money to Tellson's in advance could be found there, helping their needy friends.

raw: To which it must be added that every new-comer from France reported himself and his tidings at Tellson’s, almost as a matter of course.
en: Additionally, almost every new traveler arriving from France reported to Tellson's to share their news.

raw: For such variety of reasons, Tellson’s was at that time, as to French intelligence, a kind of High Exchange; and this was so well known to the public, and the inquiries made there were in consequence so numerous, that Tellson’s sometimes wrote the latest news out in a line or so and posted it in the Bank windows, for all who ran through Temple Bar to read.
en: For all these reasons, Tellson's was the central hub for French news, and so many people came to ask questions that the bank sometimes wrote the latest updates on a paper and posted them in the windows for anyone walking by Temple Bar to read.

raw: On a steaming, misty afternoon, Mr.
en: On a hot, misty afternoon, Mr.

raw: Lorry sat at his desk, and Charles Darnay stood leaning on it, talking with him in a low voice.
en: Lorry sat at his desk while Charles Darnay stood leaning on it, talking to him quietly.

raw: The penitential den once set apart for interviews with the House, was now the news-Exchange, and was filled to overflowing.
en: The gloomy room once used for private meetings was now packed with people exchanging news.

raw: It was within half an hour or so of the time of closing.
en: It was about half an hour before closing time.

raw: “But, although you are the youngest man that ever lived,” said Charles Darnay, rather hesitating, “I must still suggest to you--”
en: “Even though you are the most youthful-spirited man alive,” Charles Darnay said, hesitating a bit, “I still have to suggest to you, ”

raw: “I understand.
en: “I understand.

raw: That I am too old?” said Mr.
en: You think I am too old?” said Mr.

raw: Lorry.
en: Lorry.

raw: “Unsettled weather, a long journey, uncertain means of travelling, a disorganised country, a city that may not be even safe for you.”
en: “Bad weather, a long journey, unreliable transport, a chaotic country, and a city that might not even be safe for you.”

raw: “My dear Charles,” said Mr.
en: “My dear Charles,” Mr.

raw: Lorry, with cheerful confidence, “you touch some of the reasons for my going: not for my staying away.
en: Lorry said with cheerful confidence, “those are the exact reasons I must go, not stay.

raw: It is safe enough for me; nobody will care to interfere with an old fellow of hard upon fourscore when there are so many people there much better worth interfering with.
en: I will be safe enough. No one will bother an old man of nearly eighty when there are so many other people worth targeting.

raw: As to its being a disorganised city, if it were not a disorganised city there would be no occasion to send somebody from our House here to our House there, who knows the city and the business, of old, and is in Tellson’s confidence.
en: As for the chaos, if the city weren't chaotic, we wouldn't need to send someone from our London office to our Paris branch who knows the place and the business, and whom Tellson's trusts completely.

raw: As to the uncertain travelling, the long journey, and the winter weather, if I were not prepared to submit myself to a few inconveniences for the sake of Tellson’s, after all these years, who ought to be?”
en: As for the difficult travel, the long journey, and the winter weather, if I am not willing to face a few hardships for Tellson's after all these years, who should be?”

raw: “I wish I were going myself,” said Charles Darnay, somewhat restlessly, and like one thinking aloud.
en: “I wish I were going myself,” Charles Darnay said restlessly, as if thinking aloud.

raw: “Indeed!
en: “Really!

raw: You are a pretty fellow to object and advise!” exclaimed Mr.
en: You are a fine one to complain and give advice!” Mr.

raw: Lorry. “You wish you were going yourself?
en: Lorry exclaimed. “You wish you were going?

raw: And you a Frenchman born?
en: A born Frenchman?

raw: You are a wise counsellor.”
en: You are a very wise adviser indeed!”

raw: “My dear Mr.
en: “My dear Mr.

raw: Lorry, it is because I am a Frenchman born, that the thought (which I did not mean to utter here, however) has passed through my mind often.
en: Lorry, it is precisely because I am a Frenchman that the thought has crossed my mind so often, though I didn't mean to say it aloud.

raw: One cannot help thinking, having had some sympathy for the miserable people, and having abandoned something to them,” he spoke here in his former thoughtful manner, “that one might be listened to, and might have the power to persuade to some restraint.
en: Having felt sympathy for the poor people and having given up my property to them,” he spoke thoughtfully, “I cannot help but think that they might listen to me. I might be able to persuade them to show some mercy.

raw: Only last night, after you had left us, when I was talking to Lucie--”
en: Only last night, after you left, I was talking to Lucie, ”

raw: “When you were talking to Lucie,” Mr.
en: “Talking to Lucie,” Mr.

raw: Lorry repeated. “Yes.
en: Lorry repeated. “Yes!

raw: I wonder you are not ashamed to mention the name of Lucie! Wishing you were going to France at this time of day!”
en: I'm surprised you're not ashamed to mention her name while wishing you were going to France at a time like this!”

raw: “However, I am not going,” said Charles Darnay, with a smile. “It is more to the purpose that you say you are.”
en: “Well, I am not going,” Charles Darnay said with a smile. “It is more important that you are.”

raw: “And I am, in plain reality.
en: “And I really am.

raw: The truth is, my dear Charles,” Mr.
en: The truth is, my dear Charles,” Mr.

raw: Lorry glanced at the distant House, and lowered his voice, “you can have no conception of the difficulty with which our business is transacted, and of the peril in which our books and papers over yonder are involved.
en: Lorry said, looking toward the other bank managers and lowering his voice, “you have no idea how hard it is to do business there, or how much danger our records and papers are in.

raw: The Lord above knows what the compromising consequences would be to numbers of people, if some of our documents were seized or destroyed; and they might be, at any time, you know, for who can say that Paris is not set afire to-day, or sacked to-morrow!
en: God only knows what terrible trouble it would cause for many people if our documents were seized or destroyed. And that could happen at any moment, who knows if Paris will be set on fire today or looted tomorrow!

raw: Now, a judicious selection from these with the least possible delay, and the burying of them, or otherwise getting of them out of harm’s way, is within the power (without loss of precious time) of scarcely any one but myself, if any one.
en: Now, carefully choosing the important papers right away, and burying them or otherwise getting them out of harm's way, is something that hardly anyone but me can do without wasting precious time.

raw: And shall I hang back, when Tellson’s knows this and says this--Tellson’s, whose bread I have eaten these sixty years--because I am a little stiff about the joints?
en: Should I refuse, when Tellson's needs me, Tellson's, who has paid my salary for sixty years, just because my joints are a little stiff?

raw: Why, I am a boy, sir, to half a dozen old codgers here!”
en: Why, I'm a boy compared to half the old men working here!”

raw: “How I admire the gallantry of your youthful spirit, Mr.
en: “I really admire your youthful courage, Mr.

raw: Lorry.”
en: Lorry.”

raw: “Tut!
en: “Nonsense, sir!

raw: Nonsense, sir!--And, my dear Charles,” said Mr.
en: And, my dear Charles,” Mr.

raw: Lorry, glancing at the House again, “you are to remember, that getting things out of Paris at this present time, no matter what things, is next to an impossibility.
en: Lorry said, looking back at the bank managers, “you must remember that getting anything out of Paris right now is almost impossible.

raw: Papers and precious matters were this very day brought to us here (I speak in strict confidence; it is not business-like to whisper it, even to you), by the strangest bearers you can imagine, every one of whom had his head hanging on by a single hair as he passed the Barriers.
en: Just today, papers and valuables were brought to us here, I tell you this in strict confidence, as it's not professional to gossip, even to you, by the strangest messengers, who were in constant danger of losing their heads as they crossed the borders.

raw: At another time, our parcels would come and go, as easily as in business-like Old England; but now, everything is stopped.”
en: Normally, our mail would come and go as easily as in England, but now, everything is blocked.”

raw: “And do you really go to-night?”
en: “And are you really leaving tonight?”

raw: “I really go to-night, for the case has become too pressing to admit of delay.”
en: “I really am, because the situation has become too urgent to wait.”

raw: “And do you take no one with you?”
en: “Are you going alone?”

raw: “All sorts of people have been proposed to me, but I will have nothing to say to any of them.
en: “Many people were suggested to me, but I refused them all.

raw: I intend to take Jerry.
en: I plan to take Jerry.

raw: Jerry has been my bodyguard on Sunday nights for a long time past and I am used to him.
en: Jerry has been my Sunday night bodyguard for a long time, and I am used to him.

raw: Nobody will suspect Jerry of being anything but an English bull-dog, or of having any design in his head but to fly at anybody who touches his master.”
en: No one will suspect Jerry of being anything other than an English bulldog, ready to attack anyone who touches his master.”

raw: “I must say again that I heartily admire your gallantry and youthfulness.”
en: “I must say again that I truly admire your youthfulness and courage.”

raw: “I must say again, nonsense, nonsense!
en: “And I must say again, nonsense!

raw: When I have executed this little commission, I shall, perhaps, accept Tellson’s proposal to retire and live at my ease.
en: Once I finish this little job, maybe I will accept Tellson's offer to retire and live comfortably.

raw: Time enough, then, to think about growing old.”
en: That will be the time to think about getting old.”

raw: This dialogue had taken place at Mr.
en: This conversation took place at Mr.

raw: Lorry’s usual desk, with Monseigneur swarming within a yard or two of it, boastful of what he would do to avenge himself on the rascal-people before long.
en: Lorry's desk, with French aristocrats gathering just a few feet away, boasting about how they would soon get revenge on the common people.

raw: It was too much the way of Monseigneur under his reverses as a refugee, and it was much too much the way of native British orthodoxy, to talk of this terrible Revolution as if it were the only harvest ever known under the skies that had not been sown--as if nothing had ever been done, or omitted to be done, that had led to it--as if observers of the wretched millions in France, and of the misused and perverted resources that should have made them prosperous, had not seen it inevitably coming, years before, and had not in plain words recorded what they saw.
en: It was typical of the refugees, and of the conservative English public, to talk about this terrible Revolution as if it were a disaster that had come out of nowhere, as if nothing had ever been done to cause it. They ignored the fact that anyone who had observed the starving millions in France and the greed of the rulers had seen it coming years ago and warned about it in plain words.

raw: Such vapouring, combined with the extravagant plots of Monseigneur for the restoration of a state of things that had utterly exhausted itself, and worn out Heaven and earth as well as itself, was hard to be endured without some remonstrance by any sane man who knew the truth.
en: Such empty boasting, mixed with the wealthy nobles' crazy plots to bring back a way of life that had completely ruined itself and exhausted both Heaven and earth, was hard for any sane person who knew the truth to put up with without arguing back.

raw: And it was such vapouring all about his ears, like a troublesome confusion of blood in his own head, added to a latent uneasiness in his mind, which had already made Charles Darnay restless, and which still kept him so.
en: Hearing all this empty talk buzzing around his ears was like a confusing rush of blood to his head. Combined with a deep, hidden uneasiness in his mind, it had already made Charles Darnay restless, and it continued to keep him that way.

raw: Among the talkers, was Stryver, of the King’s Bench Bar, far on his way to state promotion, and, therefore, loud on the theme: broaching to Monseigneur, his devices for blowing the people up and exterminating them from the face of the earth, and doing without them: and for accomplishing many similar objects akin in their nature to the abolition of eagles by sprinkling salt on the tails of the race.
en: Among the talkers was Stryver, the ambitious lawyer, who was speaking loudly to the aristocrats. He was explaining his ideas for blowing up the French peasants and wiping them off the face of the earth, which was about as realistic as trying to catch eagles by putting salt on their tails.

raw: Him, Darnay heard with a particular feeling of objection; and Darnay stood divided between going away that he might hear no more, and remaining to interpose his word, when the thing that was to be, went on to shape itself out.
en: Darnay listened to him with disgust. He was torn between walking away to avoid hearing any more, and staying to speak up, when the next event began to unfold.

raw: The House approached Mr.
en: One of the bank managers came over to Mr.

raw: Lorry, and laying a soiled and unopened letter before him, asked if he had yet discovered any traces of the person to whom it was addressed?
en: Lorry and laid a dirty, unopened letter on the desk, asking if he had found any trace of the person to whom it was addressed.

raw: The House laid the letter down so close to Darnay that he saw the direction--the more quickly because it was his own right name.
en: The manager placed the letter so close to Darnay that he could read the address, and he recognized it immediately because it was his real name.

raw: The address, turned into English, ran:
en: The address read:

raw: “Very pressing.
en: “Very urgent.

raw: To Monsieur heretofore the Marquis St.
en: To Monsieur, formerly the Marquis St.

raw: Evrémonde, of France.
en: Evremonde, of France.

raw: Confided to the cares of Messrs.
en: Care of Messrs.

raw: Tellson and Co., Bankers, London, England.”
en: Tellson and Co., Bankers, London, England.”

raw: On the marriage morning, Doctor Manette had made it his one urgent and express request to Charles Darnay, that the secret of this name should be--unless he, the Doctor, dissolved the obligation--kept inviolate between them.
en: On the morning of his wedding, Doctor Manette had earnestly requested Charles Darnay to keep the secret of his real family name between the two of them.

raw: Nobody else knew it to be his name; his own wife had no suspicion of the fact; Mr.
en: No one else knew it. Even his wife had no idea, and Mr.

raw: Lorry could have none.
en: Lorry certainly did not know.

raw: “No,” said Mr.
en: “No,” Mr.

raw: Lorry, in reply to the House; “I have referred it, I think, to everybody now here, and no one can tell me where this gentleman is to be found.”
en: Lorry replied to the manager. “I have asked almost everyone here, and no one knows where this gentleman can be found.”

raw: The hands of the clock verging upon the hour of closing the Bank, there was a general set of the current of talkers past Mr.
en: As the bank's closing hour approached, the crowd of talkers began to move past Mr.

raw: Lorry’s desk.
en: Lorry's desk.

raw: He held the letter out inquiringly; and Monseigneur looked at it, in the person of this plotting and indignant refugee; and Monseigneur looked at it in the person of that plotting and indignant refugee; and This, That, and The Other, all had something disparaging to say, in French or in English, concerning the Marquis who was not to be found.
en: He held up the letter to show them. One angry refugee after another looked at it, and each had something insulting to say, in French or in English, about the missing Marquis.

raw: “Nephew, I believe--but in any case degenerate successor--of the polished Marquis who was murdered,” said one. “Happy to say, I never knew him.”
en: “He is the nephew, or at least the worthless successor, of the refined Marquis who was murdered,” said one. “I am glad to say I never knew him.”

raw: “A craven who abandoned his post,” said another--this Monseigneur had been got out of Paris, legs uppermost and half suffocated, in a load of hay--“some years ago.”
en: “A coward who abandoned his position years ago,” said another, a man who had himself escaped Paris hidden under a load of hay, upside down and half suffocated.

raw: “Infected with the new doctrines,” said a third, eyeing the direction through his glass in passing; “set himself in opposition to the last Marquis, abandoned the estates when he inherited them, and left them to the ruffian herd.
en: “Infected with those new revolutionary ideas,” said a third, looking at the address through his glass as he passed. “He opposed the late Marquis, abandoned his estate when he inherited it, and left it to the mob.

raw: They will recompense him now, I hope, as he deserves.”
en: I hope they reward him now as he deserves.”

raw: “Hey?” cried the blatant Stryver. “Did he though?
en: “Hey?” cried the loud Stryver. “Did he really?

raw: Is that the sort of fellow?
en: Is that the kind of guy he is?

raw: Let us look at his infamous name.
en: Let me see his shameful name.

raw: D--n the fellow!”
en: Damn him!”

raw: Darnay, unable to restrain himself any longer, touched Mr.
en: Darnay, unable to control himself any longer, touched Mr.

raw: Stryver on the shoulder, and said:
en: Stryver on the shoulder and said:

raw: “I know the fellow.”
en: “I know him.”

raw: “Do you, by Jupiter?” said Stryver. “I am sorry for it.”
en: “Do you, by Jove?” said Stryver. “I am sorry to hear that.”

raw: “Why?”
en: “Why?”

raw: “Why, Mr.
en: “Why, Mr.

raw: Darnay?
en: Darnay?

raw: D’ye hear what he did?
en: Did you hear what he did?

raw: Don’t ask, why, in these times.”
en: Don't ask why in times like these.”

raw: “But I do ask why?”
en: “But I do ask why.”

raw: “Then I tell you again, Mr.
en: “Then I tell you again, Mr.

raw: Darnay, I am sorry for it.
en: Darnay, I am sorry.

raw: I am sorry to hear you putting any such extraordinary questions.
en: I am sorry to hear you asking such strange questions.

raw: Here is a fellow, who, infected by the most pestilent and blasphemous code of devilry that ever was known, abandoned his property to the vilest scum of the earth that ever did murder by wholesale, and you ask me why I am sorry that a man who instructs youth knows him?
en: Here is a man who, influenced by the most wicked and ungodly ideas ever known, gave up his property to the worst scum of the earth who murder people wholesale. And you ask me why I'm sorry that a teacher of youth knows him?

raw: Well, but I’ll answer you.
en: Well, I will tell you.

raw: I am sorry because I believe there is contamination in such a scoundrel.
en: I'm sorry because I think such a scoundrel is contagious.

raw: That’s why.”
en: That's why.”

raw: Mindful of the secret, Darnay with great difficulty checked himself, and said: “You may not understand the gentleman.”
en: Remembering his secret, Darnay controlled himself with great effort and said, “You might not understand the gentleman.”

raw: “I understand how to put _you_ in a corner, Mr.
en: “I know how to put _you_ in a corner, Mr.

raw: Darnay,” said Bully Stryver, “and I’ll do it.
en: Darnay,” Stryver bullied, “and I'll do it.

raw: If this fellow is a gentleman, I _don’t_ understand him.
en: If that fellow is a gentleman, then I _don't_ understand him.

raw: You may tell him so, with my compliments.
en: You can tell him so, with my compliments.

raw: You may also tell him, from me, that after abandoning his worldly goods and position to this butcherly mob, I wonder he is not at the head of them.
en: You can also tell him from me that since he gave up his wealth and status to this murderous mob, I wonder he isn't leading them.

raw: But, no, gentlemen,” said Stryver, looking all round, and snapping his fingers, “I know something of human nature, and I tell you that you’ll never find a fellow like this fellow, trusting himself to the mercies of such precious _protégés_.
en: But no, gentlemen,” Stryver said, looking around and snapping his fingers, “I know a bit about human nature, and I tell you that you'll never find a guy like him trusting himself to the mercy of those people.

raw: No, gentlemen; he’ll always show ’em a clean pair of heels very early in the scuffle, and sneak away.”
en: No, gentlemen; he'll run away at the first sign of trouble and hide.”

raw: With those words, and a final snap of his fingers, Mr.
en: With those words and a final snap of his fingers, Mr.

raw: Stryver shouldered himself into Fleet-street, amidst the general approbation of his hearers.
en: Stryver pushed his way out into Fleet Street, to the general approval of the listeners.

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Lorry and Charles Darnay were left alone at the desk, in the general departure from the Bank.
en: Lorry and Charles Darnay were left alone at the desk as everyone else left the bank.

raw: “Will you take charge of the letter?” said Mr.
en: “Will you take care of this letter?” Mr.

raw: Lorry. “You know where to deliver it?”
en: Lorry asked. “Do you know where to deliver it?”

raw: “I do.”
en: “I do.”

raw: “Will you undertake to explain, that we suppose it to have been addressed here, on the chance of our knowing where to forward it, and that it has been here some time?”
en: “Will you explain to him that we think it was sent here in the hope that we would know where to find him, and that it has been sitting here for a while?”

raw: “I will do so.
en: “I will.

raw: Do you start for Paris from here?”
en: Are you leaving for Paris from here?”

raw: “From here, at eight.”
en: “From here, at eight o'clock.”

raw: “I will come back, to see you off.”
en: “I will come back to see you off.”

raw: Very ill at ease with himself, and with Stryver and most other men, Darnay made the best of his way into the quiet of the Temple, opened the letter, and read it.
en: Feeling very uncomfortable with himself, Stryver, and everyone else, Darnay walked back to the quiet of the Temple, opened the letter, and read it.

raw: These were its contents:
en: This is what it said:

raw: “Prison of the Abbaye, Paris.
en: “Abbaye Prison, Paris.”

raw: “June 21, 1792. “MONSIEUR HERETOFORE THE MARQUIS.
en: “June 21, 1792. “MONSIEUR, FORMERLY THE MARQUIS.

raw: “After having long been in danger of my life at the hands of the village, I have been seized, with great violence and indignity, and brought a long journey on foot to Paris.
en: “After being in danger for a long time at the hands of the villagers, I have been arrested with great violence and insult, and forced to walk all the way to Paris.

raw: On the road I have suffered a great deal.
en: I suffered terribly on the road.

raw: Nor is that all; my house has been destroyed--razed to the ground.
en: Not only that, but my house has been completely destroyed and flattened to the ground.

raw: “The crime for which I am imprisoned, Monsieur heretofore the Marquis, and for which I shall be summoned before the tribunal, and shall lose my life (without your so generous help), is, they tell me, treason against the majesty of the people, in that I have acted against them for an emigrant.
en: “The crime for which I am locked up, Monsieur, and for which I will be tried and executed, unless you generously help me, is, they say, treason against the people because I managed the estate of an exile.

raw: It is in vain I represent that I have acted for them, and not against, according to your commands.
en: It does no good for me to tell them that I acted in their favor, not against them, following your orders.

raw: It is in vain I represent that, before the sequestration of emigrant property, I had remitted the imposts they had ceased to pay; that I had collected no rent; that I had had recourse to no process.
en: It does no good for me to explain that, before the exile properties were seized, I had canceled the taxes they stopped paying, collected no rents, and took no legal action against anyone.

raw: The only response is, that I have acted for an emigrant, and where is that emigrant?
en: The only answer I get is that I worked for an exile, and they ask: where is that exile?

raw: “Ah! most gracious Monsieur heretofore the Marquis, where is that emigrant?
en: “Ah, most gracious Monsieur, where is that exile?

raw: I cry in my sleep where is he?
en: I cry out in my sleep, asking where he is.

raw: I demand of Heaven, will he not come to deliver me?
en: I ask Heaven: will he not come to save me?

raw: No answer.
en: There is no answer.

raw: Ah Monsieur heretofore the Marquis, I send my desolate cry across the sea, hoping it may perhaps reach your ears through the great bank of Tilson known at Paris!
en: Ah, Monsieur, I send my desperate cry across the sea, hoping it might reach your ears through the famous bank of Tellson which is known in Paris!

raw: “For the love of Heaven, of justice, of generosity, of the honour of your noble name, I supplicate you, Monsieur heretofore the Marquis, to succour and release me.
en: “For the love of Heaven, of justice, of generosity, and for the honor of your noble family name, I beg you, Monsieur, to help and free me.

raw: My fault is, that I have been true to you.
en: My only crime is that I have been faithful to you.

raw: Oh Monsieur heretofore the Marquis, I pray you be you true to me!
en: Oh, Monsieur, I pray that you will be faithful to me!

raw: “From this prison here of horror, whence I every hour tend nearer and nearer to destruction, I send you, Monsieur heretofore the Marquis, the assurance of my dolorous and unhappy service.
en: “From this horrible prison, where every hour brings me closer to death, I send you, Monsieur, my sad and miserable respects.

raw: “Your afflicted,
en: “Your suffering servant,

raw: “Gabelle.”
en: “Gabelle.”

raw: The latent uneasiness in Darnay’s mind was roused to vigourous life by this letter.
en: The quiet anxiety in Darnay's mind flared into intense life upon reading this letter.

raw: The peril of an old servant and a good one, whose only crime was fidelity to himself and his family, stared him so reproachfully in the face, that, as he walked to and fro in the Temple considering what to do, he almost hid his face from the passersby.
en: The danger facing an old and loyal servant, whose only crime was loyalty to him and his family, felt like a direct accusation. As he walked back and forth in the Temple thinking about what to do, he was so ashamed that he almost hid his face from passersby.

raw: He knew very well, that in his horror of the deed which had culminated the bad deeds and bad reputation of the old family house, in his resentful suspicions of his uncle, and in the aversion with which his conscience regarded the crumbling fabric that he was supposed to uphold, he had acted imperfectly.
en: He knew very well that in his horror at the family's past cruelty and bad reputation, in his hatred for his uncle, and in his desire to have nothing to do with the estate he was supposed to inherit, he had acted imperfectly.

raw: He knew very well, that in his love for Lucie, his renunciation of his social place, though by no means new to his own mind, had been hurried and incomplete.
en: He knew that because of his love for Lucie, his decision to give up his title and property, though not a new idea to him, had been rushed and incomplete.

raw: He knew that he ought to have systematically worked it out and supervised it, and that he had meant to do it, and that it had never been done.
en: He knew he should have systematically managed the transition and supervised it, and though he had intended to, he had never actually done it.

raw: The happiness of his own chosen English home, the necessity of being always actively employed, the swift changes and troubles of the time which had followed on one another so fast, that the events of this week annihilated the immature plans of last week, and the events of the week following made all new again; he knew very well, that to the force of these circumstances he had yielded:--not without disquiet, but still without continuous and accumulating resistance.
en: The happiness of his new English home, the need to stay busy, and the rapid pace of events in France, where the news of one week destroyed the plans of the week before, and the following week changed everything again, had overwhelmed him. He had let things drift, feeling uneasy but not doing anything to stop it.

raw: That he had watched the times for a time of action, and that they had shifted and struggled until the time had gone by, and the nobility were trooping from France by every highway and byway, and their property was in course of confiscation and destruction, and their very names were blotting out, was as well known to himself as it could be to any new authority in France that might impeach him for it.
en: He had waited for the right moment to take action, but the situation had changed so fast that the opportunity had passed. Now, the nobles were fleeing France along every road, their properties were being seized and destroyed, and their very names were being erased, facts he knew just as well as the new French authorities who might accuse him of abandonment.

raw: But, he had oppressed no man, he had imprisoned no man; he was so far from having harshly exacted payment of his dues, that he had relinquished them of his own will, thrown himself on a world with no favour in it, won his own private place there, and earned his own bread.
en: Yet, he had oppressed no one and imprisoned no one. Far from demanding high taxes or rents, he had given them up voluntarily, started a new life in England with no special help, built his own career, and earned his own living.

raw: Monsieur Gabelle had held the impoverished and involved estate on written instructions, to spare the people, to give them what little there was to give--such fuel as the heavy creditors would let them have in the winter, and such produce as could be saved from the same grip in the summer--and no doubt he had put the fact in plea and proof, for his own safety, so that it could not but appear now.
en: Monsieur Gabelle had managed the poor estate based on Darnay's written instructions to spare the people and give them whatever they could, such as winter firewood and summer crops. Gabelle would surely use these instructions to prove his innocence, so the truth would have to come out.

raw: This favoured the desperate resolution Charles Darnay had begun to make, that he would go to Paris.
en: This supported the desperate decision Charles Darnay was starting to make: he would go to Paris.

raw: Yes.
en: Yes.

raw: Like the mariner in the old story, the winds and streams had driven him within the influence of the Loadstone Rock, and it was drawing him to itself, and he must go.
en: Like the sailor in the old story, the winds and currents had driven him into the magnetic pull of the Loadstone Rock, and it was drawing him in.

raw: Everything that arose before his mind drifted him on, faster and faster, more and more steadily, to the terrible attraction.
en: He had to go. Every thought pushed him faster and more steadily toward this dangerous attraction.

raw: His latent uneasiness had been, that bad aims were being worked out in his own unhappy land by bad instruments, and that he who could not fail to know that he was better than they, was not there, trying to do something to stay bloodshed, and assert the claims of mercy and humanity.
en: His hidden guilt had been that bad deeds were being done in France by bad people, while he, who knew he had better intentions, was not there to try to stop the bloodshed and call for mercy.

raw: With this uneasiness half stifled, and half reproaching him, he had been brought to the pointed comparison of himself with the brave old gentleman in whom duty was so strong; upon that comparison (injurious to himself) had instantly followed the sneers of Monseigneur, which had stung him bitterly, and those of Stryver, which above all were coarse and galling, for old reasons.
en: With this guilt troubling him, he had compared himself to the brave old Mr. Lorry, whose sense of duty was so strong. Right after that embarrassing comparison, he had been stung by the insults of the refugees and Stryver's coarse sneers.

raw: Upon those, had followed Gabelle’s letter: the appeal of an innocent prisoner, in danger of death, to his justice, honour, and good name.
en: And finally, Gabelle's letter had arrived: an appeal from an innocent prisoner in danger of death, calling on his justice, honor, and family name.

raw: His resolution was made.
en: His decision was made.

raw: He must go to Paris.
en: He had to go to Paris.

raw: Yes. The Loadstone Rock was drawing him, and he must sail on, until he struck.
en: Yes, the Loadstone Rock was pulling him, and he had to sail on until he reached it.

raw: He knew of no rock; he saw hardly any danger.
en: He didn't see the danger.

raw: The intention with which he had done what he had done, even although he had left it incomplete, presented it before him in an aspect that would be gratefully acknowledged in France on his presenting himself to assert it.
en: He believed that his good intentions, even if incomplete, would be recognized and appreciated in France once he arrived to explain them.

raw: Then, that glorious vision of doing good, which is so often the sanguine mirage of so many good minds, arose before him, and he even saw himself in the illusion with some influence to guide this raging Revolution that was running so fearfully wild.
en: Then, the idealistic dream of doing good, which often misleads well-meaning people, filled his mind, and he even imagined himself having the influence to guide this wild, raging Revolution.

raw: As he walked to and fro with his resolution made, he considered that neither Lucie nor her father must know of it until he was gone.
en: As he walked back and forth, he decided that neither Lucie nor her father must know about his plans until he had left.

raw: Lucie should be spared the pain of separation; and her father, always reluctant to turn his thoughts towards the dangerous ground of old, should come to the knowledge of the step, as a step taken, and not in the balance of suspense and doubt.
en: Lucie should be spared the pain of a long goodbye, and her father, who always avoided thinking about his painful past in France, should only hear about the journey after it had already begun, to avoid any suspense or worry.

raw: How much of the incompleteness of his situation was referable to her father, through the painful anxiety to avoid reviving old associations of France in his mind, he did not discuss with himself.
en: Darnay did not admit to himself how much of his delay in sorting out his French estate had been due to his fear of upsetting Doctor Manette.

raw: But, that circumstance too, had had its influence in his course.
en: But that had certainly played a part in his inaction.

raw: He walked to and fro, with thoughts very busy, until it was time to return to Tellson’s and take leave of Mr.
en: He walked back and forth, his mind racing, until it was time to return to Tellson's and say goodbye to Mr.

raw: Lorry.
en: Lorry.

raw: As soon as he arrived in Paris he would present himself to this old friend, but he must say nothing of his intention now.
en: As soon as he got to Paris, he would meet his old friend, but he could say nothing about his plans now.

raw: A carriage with post-horses was ready at the Bank door, and Jerry was booted and equipped.
en: A carriage with fresh horses was ready at the bank door, and Jerry stood booted and ready.

raw: “I have delivered that letter,” said Charles Darnay to Mr.
en: “I delivered that letter,” Charles Darnay said to Mr.

raw: Lorry. “I would not consent to your being charged with any written answer, but perhaps you will take a verbal one?”
en: Lorry. “I didn't want you to carry a written reply, but perhaps you can deliver a verbal message?”

raw: “That I will, and readily,” said Mr.
en: “I will gladly do that,” Mr.

raw: Lorry, “if it is not dangerous.”
en: Lorry said, “if it isn't dangerous.”

raw: “Not at all.
en: “Not at all.

raw: Though it is to a prisoner in the Abbaye.”
en: Though it is for a prisoner in the Abbaye.”

raw: “What is his name?” said Mr.
en: “What is his name?” Mr.

raw: Lorry, with his open pocket-book in his hand.
en: Lorry asked, opening his notebook.

raw: “Gabelle.”
en: “Gabelle.”

raw: “Gabelle.
en: “Gabelle.

raw: And what is the message to the unfortunate Gabelle in prison?”
en: And what is the message for poor Gabelle in prison?”

raw: “Simply, ‘that he has received the letter, and will come.’”
en: “Simply: ‘He received the letter and will come.’”

raw: “Any time mentioned?”
en: “Did he mention when?”

raw: “He will start upon his journey to-morrow night.”
en: “He will start his journey tomorrow night.”

raw: “Any person mentioned?”
en: “Did he mention any name?”

raw: “No.”
en: “No.”

raw: He helped Mr.
en: He helped Mr.

raw: Lorry to wrap himself in a number of coats and cloaks, and went out with him from the warm atmosphere of the old Bank, into the misty air of Fleet-street. “My love to Lucie, and to little Lucie,” said Mr.
en: Lorry wrap himself in several coats and cloaks, and walked out with him from the warm bank into the misty air of Fleet Street. “Give my love to Lucie and little Lucie,” Mr.

raw: Lorry at parting, “and take precious care of them till I come back.”  Charles Darnay shook his head and doubtfully smiled, as the carriage rolled away.
en: Lorry said as they parted, “and take good care of them until I return.” Charles Darnay shook his head and smiled doubtfully as the carriage drove off.

raw: That night--it was the fourteenth of August--he sat up late, and wrote two fervent letters; one was to Lucie, explaining the strong obligation he was under to go to Paris, and showing her, at length, the reasons that he had, for feeling confident that he could become involved in no personal danger there; the other was to the Doctor, confiding Lucie and their dear child to his care, and dwelling on the same topics with the strongest assurances.
en: That night, it was August fourteenth, he stayed up late and wrote two emotional letters. One was to Lucie, explaining the heavy duty that forced him to go to Paris and explaining in detail why he was confident he would not be in any personal danger. The other was to the Doctor, entrusting Lucie and their child to his care and repeating the same strong reassurances.

raw: To both, he wrote that he would despatch letters in proof of his safety, immediately after his arrival.
en: He promised both of them that he would send letters proving his safety as soon as he arrived.

raw: It was a hard day, that day of being among them, with the first reservation of their joint lives on his mind.
en: It had been a difficult day, spending it with his family while keeping this major secret from them for the first time in their marriage.

raw: It was a hard matter to preserve the innocent deceit of which they were profoundly unsuspicious.
en: It was hard to keep up the innocent deception, which they did not suspect at all.

raw: But, an affectionate glance at his wife, so happy and busy, made him resolute not to tell her what impended (he had been half moved to do it, so strange it was to him to act in anything without her quiet aid), and the day passed quickly.
en: But looking affectionately at his happy, busy wife, he remained resolved not to tell her what was happening, though he had been tempted to, since it felt so strange to do anything without her quiet support. The day went by quickly.

raw: Early in the evening he embraced her, and her scarcely less dear namesake, pretending that he would return by-and-bye (an imaginary engagement took him out, and he had secreted a valise of clothes ready), and so he emerged into the heavy mist of the heavy streets, with a heavier heart.
en: Early in the evening, he hugged her and their daughter, pretending he would be back soon, making up excuse to go out, having already hidden a small suitcase of clothes. And so he stepped out into the thick mist of the heavy streets with an even heavier heart.

raw: The unseen force was drawing him fast to itself, now, and all the tides and winds were setting straight and strong towards it.
en: The unseen force was drawing him in quickly now, and all the winds and tides were pushing him directly toward it.

raw: He left his two letters with a trusty porter, to be delivered half an hour before midnight, and no sooner; took horse for Dover; and began his journey. “For the love of Heaven, of justice, of generosity, of the honour of your noble name!” was the poor prisoner’s cry with which he strengthened his sinking heart, as he left all that was dear on earth behind him, and floated away for the Loadstone Rock. The end of the second book.
en: He left his two letters with a trusted messenger, to be delivered exactly half an hour before midnight and no earlier. Then he took a horse for Dover and began his journey. “For the love of Heaven, of justice, of generosity, and for the honor of your noble name!” was the poor prisoner's cry that he repeated to strengthen his failing courage, as he left everything he loved behind and floated toward the Loadstone Rock.

raw: Book the Third--the Track of a Storm
en: The end of the second book.
